metadata.summary: This evidence-based guideline addresses the evaluation and management of giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis. It covers diagnostic testing, vascular imaging, pharmacologic treatment, vascular surgery, and clinical and laboratory monitoring. Most recommendations are conditional because the available evidence is limited.

management.severity: Significant risk of severe glucocorticoid toxicity
management.actions: For GCA, moderate-dose oral glucocorticoids may be used when the risk of vision loss or other life- or organ-threatening complications is low.

prevention: After initiating high-dose oral glucocorticoids for GCA, taper the dose over weeks to months to avoid prolonged high-dose treatment.
For TAK, limit glucocorticoid exposure when possible.
toxicities.dose_modifications: For TAK in remission after receiving glucocorticoids for ≥6–12 months, tapering them off is conditionally recommended over prolonged low-dose treatment; longer treatment may be needed if disease control is inadequate or relapses are frequent.

prevention: For newly diagnosed GCA without cranial ischemia, high-dose oral glucocorticoids are conditionally preferred to routine IV pulse glucocorticoids; risks associated with pulse treatment, including infections, may outweigh its benefits, particularly in older patients.

For children with TAK, alternative steroid schedules, such as IV pulse glucocorticoids with a low daily oral dose, may be preferred to improve adherence and potentially reduce adverse effects on growth.
In TAK, use antiplatelet therapy cautiously after surgery or when bleeding risk is elevated.

prophylaxis.recommendation: For GCA with critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid artery involvement, adding aspirin is conditionally recommended; its antiplatelet effect may help prevent ischemic events.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with GCA and critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid artery involvement

prophylaxis.recommendation: For active TAK with critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement, adding aspirin or another antiplatelet therapy is conditionally recommended. Small observational studies suggest fewer ischemic events but more bleeding with antiplatelet therapy.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with active TAK and critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement

therapies_index.name: glucocorticoids
approved_indications: The principal treatment for GCA.
Treatment of TAK, generally alongside a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent when TAK is active.
therapies_index.administration: The dose, route and duration depend on the disease presentation and treatment context; specified schedules are indexed separately.
key_toxicities: Treatment-related toxicity motivates limiting exposure when possible.

therapies_index.name: IV methylprednisolone
approved_indications: An agent specified for IV pulse GCs.
therapies_index.administration: 500–1,000 mg/day in adults or 30 mg/kg/day in children (maximum 1,000 mg/day), for 3–5 days.

therapies_index.name: Prednisone
approved_indications: An agent specified for high-dose, moderate-dose and low-dose oral GCs.
therapies_index.administration: High dose: 1 mg/kg/day up to 80 mg; moderate dose: 0.5 mg/kg/day (generally 10–40 mg/day in adults); low dose: ≤10 mg/day.

therapies_index.name: IV pulse GCs
approved_indications: Conditionally preferred to high-dose oral glucocorticoids for newly diagnosed GCA with threatened vision loss.
May be considered for life- or organ-threatening TAK; an alternative pediatric schedule may be preferred in some children.
therapies_index.administration: IV methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg/day in adults or 30 mg/kg/day in children (maximum 1,000 mg/day), or equivalent, for 3–5 days.
key_toxicities: Routine use in GCA without cranial ischemia may increase risks, including infection, particularly in older patients.

therapies_index.name: High-dose oral GCs
approved_indications: Conditionally preferred initial treatment for newly diagnosed GCA without cranial ischemia and for active, severe TAK in patients not receiving immunosuppressive therapy.
Conditionally preferred to moderate-dose oral GCs as initial treatment for newly diagnosed GCA.
Recommended around vascular intervention when GCA or TAK is active or active disease is a concern.
therapies_index.administration: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day up to 80 mg, or equivalent. For initial GCA treatment, subsequent dose reduction over weeks to months is advised to avoid prolonged high-dose exposure.
key_toxicities: Prolonged high-dose exposure increases glucocorticoid-related toxicity.

therapies_index.name: Moderate-dose oral GCs
approved_indications: May be used for GCA when the risk of severe glucocorticoid toxicity is substantial and the risk of vision loss or other life- or organ-threatening complications is low.
therapies_index.administration: Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day (generally 10–40 mg/day in adults), or equivalent.

therapies_index.name: Low-dose oral GCs
approved_indications: Described as a possible longer-term option for TAK when disease control is inadequate or relapses are frequent; after remission on GCs for ≥6–12 months, tapering off is conditionally preferred to long-term low-dose maintenance.

therapies_index.name: oral glucocorticoids with tocilizumab
approved_indications: Conditionally preferred to oral glucocorticoids alone for newly diagnosed GCA.
therapies_index.administration: Oral glucocorticoids combined with tocilizumab; no combination dose or duration is specified.

therapies_index.name: methotrexate with glucocorticoids
approved_indications: An initial treatment option that may be considered for newly diagnosed GCA.

therapies_index.name: tocilizumab
approved_indications: Approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for GCA.
Conditionally preferred with oral glucocorticoids to oral glucocorticoids alone for newly diagnosed GCA.
May be considered for active extracranial large-vessel GCA alongside glucocorticoids.
Conditionally preferred to methotrexate, with an increased glucocorticoid dose, for GCA relapse with cranial symptoms while receiving glucocorticoids.

May be considered for TAK after an inadequate response to other immunosuppressive therapies or when tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are contraindicated; other nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive therapies are conditionally preferred for initial TAK treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous and IV formulations are discussed; no dose or schedule is specified.
monitoring: In TAK, its effect on acute-phase reactants may complicate assessment of disease activity.

therapies_index.name: methotrexate
approved_indications: May be considered with glucocorticoids for newly diagnosed GCA or active extracranial large-vessel GCA, including when tocilizumab cannot be used.
A nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive option for GCA relapse with cranial ischemic symptoms.
Often used as the initial nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent for active TAK and often preferred for children.
therapies_index.administration: Described as an oral therapy for GCA; no dose or schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: azathioprine
approved_indications: A nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive option that may be considered with glucocorticoids for active TAK.

therapies_index.name: Abatacept
approved_indications: May be considered with glucocorticoids for GCA if the other agents discussed for initial treatment are ineffective.

therapies_index.name: tumor necrosis factor inhibitor
approved_indications: An option alongside glucocorticoids for active TAK.
Conditionally preferred to adding tocilizumab when TAK is refractory to glucocorticoids alone.

therapies_index.name: aspirin
therapies_index.mechanism: Its antiplatelet activity may help prevent ischemic events when vascular narrowing reduces cerebral blood flow.
approved_indications: Conditionally recommended as an addition for GCA with critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid artery involvement.
Conditionally recommended as an antiplatelet option for active TAK with critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement.

therapies_index.name: another antiplatelet therapy
approved_indications: Conditionally recommended as an alternative to aspirin for active TAK with critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement.
key_toxicities: Small observational studies suggest an increased bleeding risk with antiplatelet therapy.
monitoring: Use cautiously after surgery or when bleeding risk is increased.

therapies_index.name: antihypertensive drugs
approved_indications: Part of medical management for TAK with renovascular hypertension and renal artery stenosis.

therapies_index.name: surgical intervention
approved_indications: May be considered for GCA with an aortic aneurysm at high risk of rupture or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction or damage.

May be considered for TAK when limb claudication substantially restricts activity, when coronary artery involvement or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction warrants immediate intervention, or for selected vascular lesions and medically refractory renovascular hypertension.
therapies_index.administration: For vascular surgery, the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist should jointly determine the procedure and its timing. In TAK, delaying intervention until disease is quiescent is conditionally preferred when possible.
key_toxicities: The guideline describes substantial surgical risks for asymptomatic cranial or cervical stenosis involving a single vessel in TAK.

conditions.name: GCA
conditions.description: Systemic vasculitis that predominantly involves large- and medium-sized vessels. It may affect cranial arteries, extracranial large vessels, or both.
conditions.epidemiology: More common among people of Northern European descent who are older than 50 years.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Cranial features include headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss and neurologic ischemia, including amaurosis fugax or stroke. Extracranial arterial stenoses and aneurysms may cause absent pulses or limb claudication. Constitutional symptoms and symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica may also occur.

subtypes.name: cranial GCA
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Cranial involvement may produce headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or ischemic visual and neurologic manifestations. Suspected cranial disease is primarily investigated with temporal artery biopsy in the US.

subtypes.name: extracranial GCA
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Large-vessel involvement may produce stenoses or aneurysms, with findings such as absent pulses or limb claudication. Vascular imaging can establish the extent of involvement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess symptoms and signs compatible with GCA and determine whether other conditions explain them.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When GCA is suspected; also used with vascular imaging after a negative temporal artery biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New or worsening clinical findings attributable to GCA may indicate active disease; manifestations caused by prior damage do not establish current activity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify histopathologic evidence supporting a diagnosis of GCA.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For suspected GCA; initially biopsy one side, with bilateral sampling considered when symptoms are not clearly confined to 1 temporal artery or when the first biopsy is negative and further evidence of cranial disease is needed. A specimen >1 cm is preferred to one <1 cm. Obtain it as soon as possible, preferably within 2 weeks after oral glucocorticoids are started.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Because lesions can be focal, a shorter specimen can miss disease. Histopathologic findings may still be present in biopsies obtained later than 2 weeks after glucocorticoid initiation; a negative result can prompt large-vessel imaging alongside clinical assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess temporal arteries for diagnostic evidence of GCA.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May complement biopsy at centers with suitable training and expertise.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Results depend on operator expertise, and inflammatory findings can disappear quickly after glucocorticoid treatment. The guideline favors biopsy for diagnosis in the US.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for cranial vascular findings that may support a GCA diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Can contribute to diagnostic assessment, although biopsy is preferred for suspected GCA in the US.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Limited US expertise and insufficient widespread validation constrain its use as a replacement for temporal artery biopsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect extracranial large-vessel involvement and provide a baseline for comparison with later imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At new diagnosis, or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after a negative temporal artery biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Large-vessel abnormalities may provide further evidence of GCA; subsequent studies can assess stenoses, aneurysms and lesion stability.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify extracranial large-vessel disease and establish a baseline for later comparison.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At new diagnosis, or when temporal artery biopsy is negative and the diagnosis remains uncertain.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings may support extracranial GCA and permit assessment of vascular complications on subsequent imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Seek additional evidence of large-vessel involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered when a negative temporal artery biopsy leaves the diagnosis uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Seek imaging evidence of large-vessel disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered when temporal artery biopsy is negative and diagnostic uncertainty remains.

diagnostic_workup.test: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide inflammation-marker results for clinical assessment and monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An isolated increase is nonspecific and does not, by itself, warrant escalation of immunosuppressive therapy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to clinical assessment of vascular disease.

follow_up.schedule: Long-term clinical monitoring is strongly recommended during apparent remission. Its optimal frequency and duration are not established; considerations include time in remission, vascular sites involved, progression risk, immunosuppressive treatment and the patient's ability to report new symptoms. Whether patients without large-vessel involvement need repeated vascular imaging is uncertain.
recommended_tests: History and clinical examination for new signs or symptoms of active disease.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level, interpreted alongside the clinical assessment.
Blood pressures in 4 extremities as part of clinical monitoring.
Imaging studies when indicated; with known large-vessel involvement, noninvasive vascular imaging can assess stenoses, aneurysms and stability of existing lesions.
More frequent clinical and/or radiographic assessment may be appropriate when inflammation markers rise without other evidence of disease activity.
long_term_effects: Large-vessel involvement may result in aneurysms or stenoses.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: An isolated rise in inflammation markers calls for observation and monitoring rather than automatic escalation of immunosuppression. The guideline also emphasizes limiting glucocorticoid exposure because of toxicity.

conditions.name: TAK
conditions.description: Systemic vasculitis characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and its branches, principally affecting large- and medium-sized vessels.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause constitutional symptoms, raised inflammation markers, arterial stenoses or aneurysms, limb claudication and absent pulses. Vascular involvement can also cause limb or organ ischemia and renovascular hypertension.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate symptoms and signs of disease activity or vascular complications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During routine assessment and long-term monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clinical quiescence does not exclude new vascular changes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to clinical assessment of vascular disease.

diagnostic_workup.test: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Add inflammation markers to clinical assessment of disease activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During clinical monitoring, including apparent remission.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These markers are imperfect measures of activity. A rise in isolation can be nonspecific and does not necessarily justify intensifying immunosuppression.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess vascular abnormalities and possible vessel-wall inflammation without catheterization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For disease-activity assessment and scheduled imaging alongside clinical evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New stenosis, vascular edema, contrast enhancement or increased wall thickness may suggest activity, but vessel-wall abnormalities are not necessarily specific for inflammation. The clinical importance of edema or enhancement remains uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate vascular lesions and possible vessel-wall inflammation without catheterization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For disease-activity assessment and regularly scheduled imaging.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New stenosis, edema, enhancement or wall thickening may suggest activity, but imaging abnormalities require clinical interpretation and are not necessarily specific for active inflammation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess vascular-wall findings relevant to disease activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As a noninvasive imaging option for disease-activity assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Supraphysiologic FDG uptake in the arterial wall is an imaging finding of activity, although the clinical significance of vascular imaging abnormalities is not fully established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the vascular lumen, measure central blood pressures accurately or assist surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When noninvasive imaging is inadequate, central pressure measurement is needed or an intervention is being planned.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It primarily depicts the lumen rather than vascular-wall inflammation; noninvasive imaging is preferred for assessment of disease activity.

follow_up.schedule: Long-term clinical monitoring is strongly recommended in apparent remission. The interval depends on remission duration, involved sites, progression risk, immunosuppressive treatment and the patient's ability to report new findings. The optimal imaging interval is uncertain; intervals described include every 3–6 months or longer, potentially shorter early in the disease course and longer once disease is established and quiescent.
recommended_tests: Routine clinical assessment, including symptoms, examination and blood pressures in 4 extremities.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level as adjuncts to clinical monitoring.
Regularly scheduled noninvasive vascular imaging in addition to routine clinical assessment.
Consider more frequent clinical and/or radiographic evaluation if inflammation markers rise during apparent remission.
Review imaging abnormalities with a radiologist before deciding whether they represent active disease.
long_term_effects: Arterial stenoses or aneurysms may cause ischemic complications.
Vascular lesions can progress even when disease appears clinically quiescent.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Progression of a previously identified lesion without signs of inflammation does not necessarily indicate active disease. For children with inactive disease, the clinician determines whether to perform routine imaging after weighing the potential risks and complications of sedation against its benefits.

special_populations.considerations: For TAK, treatment choices may account for growth and adherence. Imaging may require sedation, which carries risks; the treating clinician weighs those risks against the benefits of routine imaging when disease is inactive.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The definition of IV pulse GCs specifies 30 mg/kg/day for children (maximum 1,000 mg/day) or equivalent for 3–5 days. In severe TAK, an alternative such as IV pulse glucocorticoids with a low daily oral dose may be preferred to support adherence and potentially lessen effects on growth. Methotrexate is often preferred as an initial nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent in children because it is usually well tolerated.

special_populations.considerations: Routine IV pulse glucocorticoids may carry risks, including infection, that outweigh possible benefits, particularly in older patients.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For newly diagnosed GCA without cranial ischemia, the guideline conditionally favors high-dose oral glucocorticoids over IV pulse glucocorticoids.

special_populations.population: Patients at substantial risk of severe glucocorticoid toxicity
special_populations.considerations: Initial glucocorticoid dosing can take account of toxicity risk alongside the likelihood of vision loss or other life- or organ-threatening complications.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Moderate-dose oral glucocorticoids may be used when severe glucocorticoid toxicity is a substantial risk and the risk of vision loss or other life- or organ-threatening complications is low.

special_populations.considerations: Recurrent infections, a history of gastrointestinal perforations or diverticulitis, and cost may limit tocilizumab use in GCA.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Methotrexate may be considered instead of tocilizumab for active extracranial large-vessel involvement or relapse with cranial symptoms when tocilizumab cannot be used or accessed.

special_populations.population: Patients with contraindications to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors
special_populations.considerations: For TAK refractory to glucocorticoids alone, the guideline conditionally favors a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor over tocilizumab but recognizes that the former may be contraindicated.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Tocilizumab may be considered when tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are contraindicated.

special_populations.population: Patients with increased bleeding risk or following surgery
special_populations.considerations: In active TAK with critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement, antiplatelet treatment may reduce ischemic events but may increase bleeding.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use antiplatelet therapy cautiously after surgical procedures or when bleeding risk is increased.

special_populations.population: Patients with factors affecting immunosuppressant selection
special_populations.considerations: In TAK, alcohol use, plans for childbearing, medication adherence, and medical comorbidities may influence which immunosuppressive agent is chosen.

artifacts.title: Table 3. Recommendations/statements for treatment (medical management and surgical intervention) and clinical/laboratory monitoring in GCA*
artifacts.source_heading: Recommendations and ungraded position statements for the management of GCA

columns: GCA PICO question informing recommendation and discussion
rows: Recommendation: For patients with newly diagnosed GCA without manifestations of cranial ischemia, we conditionally recommend initiating treatment with high-dose oral GCs over IV pulse GCs.
Recommendation: For patients with newly diagnosed GCA with threatened vision loss, we conditionally recommend initiating treatment with IV pulse GCs over high-dose oral GCs.
Recommendation: For patients with newly diagnosed GCA, we conditionally recommend dosing oral GCs daily over an alternate-day schedule.
Recommendation: For patients with newly diagnosed GCA, we conditionally recommend initiating treatment with high-dose oral GCs over moderate-dose oral GCs.
Recommendation: For patients with newly diagnosed GCA, we conditionally recommend the use of oral GCs with tocilizumab over oral GCs alone.

Recommendation: For patients with GCA with active extracranial large vessel involvement, we conditionally recommend treatment with oral GCs combined with a non-GC immunosuppressive agent over oral GCs alone.
Ungraded position statement: The optimal duration of therapy with GCs for GCA is not well established and should be guided by the patient’s values and preferences.
Recommendation: In patients with newly diagnosed GCA, we conditionally recommend against the use of an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (“statin”) specifically for the treatment of GCA.
Recommendation: For patients with GCA who have critical or flow-limiting involvement of the vertebral or carotid arteries, we conditionally recommend adding aspirin.
Recommendation: For patients with GCA who experience disease relapse while receiving moderate-to-high–dose GCs, we conditionally recommend adding a non-GC immunosuppressive drug.

Recommendation: For patients with GCA who experience disease relapse with symptoms of cranial ischemia, we conditionally recommend adding a non-GC immunosuppressive agent and increasing the dose of GCs over increasing the dose of GCs alone.

Recommendation: For patients with GCA who experience disease relapse with symptoms of cranial ischemia while receiving GCs, we conditionally recommend adding tocilizumab and increasing the dose of GCs over adding methotrexate and increasing the dose of GCs.

Ungraded position statement: For any patient requiring surgical vascular intervention for GCA, the type and timing of intervention should be a collaborative decision between the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist.

Recommendation: For patients with severe GCA and worsening signs of limb/organ ischemia who are receiving immunosuppressive therapy, we conditionally recommend escalating immunosuppressive therapy over surgical intervention with escalation of immunosuppressive therapy.

Recommendation: For patients with GCA undergoing vascular surgical intervention, we conditionally recommend the use of high-dose GCs during the periprocedural period, if the patient has active disease.
Recommendation: For patients with GCA in apparent clinical remission, we strongly recommend long-term clinical monitoring over no clinical monitoring.

Recommendation: For patients with GCA who have an increase in levels of inflammation markers alone, we conditionally recommend clinical observation and monitoring without escalation of immunosuppressive therapy.

artifacts.title: Table 4. Recommendations/statement for treatment (medical management and surgical intervention) in TAK*
artifacts.source_heading: Recommendations and ungraded position statement for the management of TAK

columns: TAK PICO question informing recommendation and discussion
rows: Recommendation: For patients with active, severe TAK who are not receiving immunosuppressive therapy, we conditionally recommend initiating treatment with high-dose oral GCs over IV pulse GCs followed by high-dose oral GCs.
Recommendation: For patients with newly active, severe TAK, we conditionally recommend initiating treatment with high-dose GCs over low-dose GCs.

Recommendation: For patients with TAK who achieved remission while receiving GCs for ≥6–12 months, we conditionally recommend tapering off GCs over long-term treatment with low-dose GCs for remission maintenance.
Recommendation: For patients with active TAK, we conditionally recommend the use of a non-GC immunosuppressive agent plus GCs over GCs alone.
Recommendation: For patients with active TAK, we conditionally recommend the use of other non-GC immunosuppressive therapy over tocilizumab as initial therapy.
Recommendation: For patients with TAK that is refractory to treatment with GCs alone, we conditionally recommend adding a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor over adding tocilizumab.

Recommendation: For patients with TAK and asymptomatic progression of a previously identified vascular lesion seen on imaging, without evidence of inflammation, we conditionally recommend continuing current therapy over escalating/changing immunosuppressive therapy.
Recommendation: For patients with active TAK and critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement, we conditionally recommend adding aspirin or another antiplatelet therapy.

Ungraded position statement: For any patient requiring surgical vascular intervention, the type and timing of intervention should be a collaborative decision between the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist.
Recommendation: In patients with known TAK and persistent limb claudication without evidence of ongoing active disease, we conditionally recommend against surgical intervention.

Recommendation: For patients with known TAK with worsening signs of limb/organ ischemia while receiving immunosuppressive therapy, we conditionally recommend escalating immunosuppressive therapy over surgical intervention with escalation of immunosuppressive therapy.
Recommendation: For patients with TAK with renovascular hypertension and renal artery stenosis, we conditionally recommend medical management over surgical intervention.
Recommendation: For patients with TAK and stenosis of a cranial/cervical vessel without clinical symptoms, we conditionally recommend medical management over surgical intervention.

Recommendation: For patients with TAK with worsening signs of limb/organ ischemia, we conditionally recommend delaying surgical intervention until the disease is quiescent over performing surgical intervention while the patient has active disease.
Recommendation: For patients with TAK who are undergoing surgical intervention, we conditionally recommend the use of high-dose GCs in the periprocedure period if the patient has active disease.

Recommendation: For patients with TAK in apparent clinical remission but with an increase in levels of inflammation markers, we conditionally recommend clinical observation without escalation of immunosuppressive therapy.
Recommendation: For patients with TAK, we conditionally recommend the use of noninvasive imaging over catheter-based dye angiography as a disease activity assessment tool.
Recommendation: For patients with known TAK, we conditionally recommend regularly scheduled noninvasive imaging in addition to routine clinical assessment.

Recommendation: For patients with TAK in apparent clinical remission but with signs of inflammation in new vascular territories (e.g., new stenosis or vessel wall thickening) on vascular imaging, we conditionally recommend treatment with immunosuppressive therapy.

artifacts.description: The table separates clinical and laboratory monitoring from vascular imaging and supplies a PICO reference and evidence level for each recommendation.
artifacts.summary: Covers assessment of TAK activity and remission through clinical monitoring, inflammation markers, and vascular imaging.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Differentiates an isolated rise in inflammation markers from new vascular findings when considering whether to change immunosuppressive therapy.

recommendations.statement: For suspected GCA, an initial biopsy of one temporal artery is conditionally preferred to biopsies of both arteries.
recommendations.context: Biopsy of both arteries may be appropriate when symptoms do not clearly localize to 1 temporal artery, or when an initial negative result leaves a need for further evidence of cranial GCA.
recommendations.rationale: A unilateral biopsy is the preferred initial approach, while the circumstances described may justify examining the other side.

recommendations.statement: For suspected GCA, a temporal artery biopsy segment >1 cm is conditionally preferred to a segment <1 cm.
recommendations.rationale: The disease can affect discrete arterial segments, so a shorter specimen may miss diagnostic changes; obtaining a longer specimen adds little morbidity.

recommendations.statement: For suspected GCA, obtaining a temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks after starting oral glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to waiting longer than 2 weeks.
recommendations.context: A later biopsy can still be informative and may be considered by the physician and patient.
recommendations.rationale: Earlier sampling increases the likelihood of identifying histopathologic changes, although such changes can persist beyond 2 weeks.

recommendations.statement: For suspected GCA, temporal artery biopsy is conditionally preferred to temporal artery ultrasound for establishing the diagnosis.
recommendations.context: At centers with suitable training and expertise, ultrasound may complement diagnostic evaluation.
recommendations.rationale: In the US, experience with this ultrasound application is comparatively limited; results depend on the operator and can change rapidly after glucocorticoid treatment.

recommendations.statement: For suspected GCA, temporal artery biopsy is conditionally preferred to MRI of the cranial arteries for establishing the diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: Limited US expertise and insufficient widespread validation currently constrain use of cranial-vessel MRI as a replacement for biopsy.

recommendations.statement: For suspected GCA with a negative temporal artery biopsy result or results, noninvasive imaging of the large vessels together with clinical assessment is conditionally preferred to clinical assessment alone.
recommendations.rationale: Large-vessel imaging may reveal further evidence of disease when the diagnosis remains uncertain after a negative biopsy.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA, noninvasive vascular imaging to assess large-vessel involvement is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: Subsequent routine imaging may help monitor identified large-vessel disease; its necessity without such involvement is uncertain.
recommendations.rationale: Baseline imaging can identify large-vessel disease and provide a comparison for later assessment of lesions and complications.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA without cranial ischemic manifestations, starting high-dose oral glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to starting IV pulse glucocorticoids.
recommendations.rationale: Routine IV pulse treatment may carry risks, including infection, that outweigh possible benefits, particularly in older patients.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA with threatened vision loss, starting IV pulse glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to starting high-dose oral glucocorticoids.
recommendations.context: The decision should take account of clinical circumstances and patient values and preferences.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence concerning IV pulse treatment in cranial ischemia is conflicting, but patients at greatest risk face potential vision loss.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA, daily oral glucocorticoid administration is conditionally preferred to administration on alternate days.
recommendations.rationale: The available evidence indicates higher remission rates with daily dosing; the panel identified no circumstance favoring alternate-day prednisone.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA, starting high-dose oral glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to starting moderate-dose oral glucocorticoids.
recommendations.context: Moderate-dose treatment may be used when the risk of severe glucocorticoid toxicity is substantial and the risk of vision loss or other life- or organ-threatening complications is low.
recommendations.rationale: A high starting dose is intended to control disease rapidly, followed by tapering to limit toxicity; evidence supporting moderate-dose treatment as initial therapy is of low quality.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA, oral glucocorticoids combined with tocilizumab are conditionally preferred to oral glucocorticoids alone.
recommendations.context: methotrexate with glucocorticoids or glucocorticoids alone may also be considered initially, according to clinical circumstances and patient preferences.
recommendations.rationale: A trial found a significant glucocorticoid-sparing effect with tocilizumab; cost and limited long-term follow-up data may restrict its use.

recommendations.statement: For GCA with active extracranial large-vessel involvement, oral glucocorticoids combined with a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent are conditionally preferred to oral glucocorticoids alone.
recommendations.context: methotrexate may be considered when tocilizumab cannot be used, including because of recurrent infections, a history of gastrointestinal perforations or diverticulitis, or cost.
recommendations.rationale: Additional immunosuppression may address active extracranial disease, although few high-quality studies evaluate these agents in this population.

recommendations.statement: The optimal duration of glucocorticoid treatment for GCA is not established; treatment duration should reflect the patient's values and preferences.
recommendations.context: Clinical manifestations, treatment toxicity, flares and clinician experience may also influence duration.
recommendations.rationale: Patients emphasized minimizing glucocorticoid exposure while recognizing that longer treatment may be needed to avoid flares.

recommendations.statement: For newly diagnosed GCA, use of an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor specifically to treat GCA is conditionally discouraged.
recommendations.context: Whether a statin is warranted to reduce cardiovascular risk is a separate question based on the patient's cardiovascular risk factors.
recommendations.rationale: Statins are not known to have a clinically significant immunosuppressive effect in GCA.

recommendations.statement: For GCA with critical or flow-limiting involvement of the vertebral or carotid arteries, adding aspirin is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: Its efficacy for preventing ischemic events without vertebral or carotid narrowing remains unclear.
recommendations.rationale: Despite limited data, aspirin's antiplatelet action may help prevent ischemic events when arterial narrowing reduces cerebral blood flow.

recommendations.statement: For GCA that relapses during moderate-to-high–dose glucocorticoid treatment, adding a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive drug is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.rationale: Relapse at these doses suggests that tapering glucocorticoids to a low dose is unlikely without glucocorticoid-sparing treatment.

recommendations.statement: For GCA relapse accompanied by cranial ischemic symptoms, adding a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent and increasing glucocorticoids are conditionally preferred to increasing glucocorticoids alone.
recommendations.context: A relapse with polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms may instead be controlled by increasing glucocorticoids alone.
recommendations.rationale: tocilizumab and methotrexate are among the nonglucocorticoid agents considered for a relapse with cranial ischemia.

recommendations.statement: For GCA relapse with cranial ischemic symptoms during glucocorticoid treatment, adding tocilizumab while increasing glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to adding methotrexate while increasing glucocorticoids.
recommendations.context: methotrexate remains an option when tocilizumab cannot be tolerated or accessed.
recommendations.rationale: Although direct comparative studies are lacking, the reported glucocorticoid-sparing effect of methotrexate is smaller than that seen with tocilizumab.

recommendations.statement: When vascular surgery is required for GCA, the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist should decide together on the procedure and its timing.

For severe GCA with worsening limb or organ ischemia despite immunosuppressive treatment, intensifying immunosuppression alone is conditionally preferred to combining surgical intervention with intensified immunosuppression.
recommendations.context: Immediate surgery may merit consideration for an aortic aneurysm at high risk of rupture or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction or damage.
recommendations.rationale: Collateral vessels may develop and improve distal blood flow.

recommendations.statement: For GCA requiring vascular surgery, high-dose glucocorticoids during the periprocedural period are conditionally recommended if disease is active.
recommendations.context: The discussion also supports perioperative high-dose oral glucocorticoids when the clinician is concerned that disease may be active.
recommendations.rationale: Direct data for GCA are limited, so support for this approach draws in part on its use in TAK.

recommendations.statement: For GCA in apparent clinical remission, long-term clinical monitoring is strongly recommended rather than no monitoring.
recommendations.context: The appropriate frequency and duration have not been established.
recommendations.rationale: Monitoring carries minimal risk, whereas failing to monitor could have catastrophic consequences.

recommendations.statement: For GCA with an isolated rise in inflammation markers, clinical observation and monitoring without intensifying immunosuppression are conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: More frequent clinical or imaging assessment for active disease may be warranted.
recommendations.rationale: Inflammation markers can rise for nonspecific reasons; an isolated increase does not warrant escalation of immunosuppression.

recommendations.statement: For active, severe TAK in a patient not receiving immunosuppression, starting high-dose oral glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to IV pulse glucocorticoids followed by high-dose oral glucocorticoids.
recommendations.context: IV pulse treatment may be considered for life- or organ-threatening disease. Alternative steroid schedules may be preferable in children to improve adherence and potentially limit adverse effects on growth.
recommendations.rationale: The guide identifies no evidence that IV pulse treatment is more effective in this setting.

recommendations.statement: For newly active, severe TAK, starting high-dose glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to starting low-dose glucocorticoids.
recommendations.context: Lower doses may be considered for newly active, nonsevere disease.
recommendations.rationale: Severe disease carries a risk of organ damage or life-threatening events.

recommendations.statement: For TAK in remission after ≥6–12 months of glucocorticoid treatment, tapering glucocorticoids to discontinuation is conditionally preferred to long-term low-dose glucocorticoids for remission maintenance.
recommendations.context: Longer treatment may be needed when disease control is inadequate or relapses are frequent.
recommendations.rationale: The optimal treatment duration is unknown, and limiting glucocorticoid exposure may reduce toxicity.

recommendations.statement: For active TAK, a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent plus glucocorticoids is conditionally preferred to glucocorticoids alone.
recommendations.context: Glucocorticoid monotherapy may be considered for mild disease or an uncertain diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: Adding a nonglucocorticoid agent is intended to reduce glucocorticoid-related toxicity.

recommendations.statement: For active TAK, nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive treatments other than tocilizumab are conditionally preferred as initial therapy.
recommendations.context: tocilizumab may be considered after an inadequate response to other immunosuppressive treatments.
recommendations.rationale: The efficacy of tocilizumab in TAK is not established; the primary efficacy endpoint was not met in the randomized trial cited by the guide.

recommendations.statement: For TAK refractory to glucocorticoids alone, adding a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor is conditionally preferred to adding tocilizumab.
recommendations.context: tocilizumab may still be considered, particularly if tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are contraindicated.
recommendations.rationale: The panel identified more clinical experience and data for tumor necrosis factor inhibitors in TAK. A randomized trial showed a nonsignificant trend toward longer time to relapse with tocilizumab and was considered underpowered.

recommendations.statement: For TAK with asymptomatic progression of a previously identified vascular lesion on imaging but no evidence of inflammation, continuing current treatment is conditionally preferred to escalating or changing immunosuppression.
recommendations.context: Escalation may be warranted if substantial progression occurs rapidly after a stable period.
recommendations.rationale: A lesion may progress for reasons unrelated to active inflammation, and collateral circulation can develop.

recommendations.statement: For active TAK with critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement, adding aspirin or another antiplatelet treatment is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: Use warrants caution after surgery or when bleeding risk is increased.
recommendations.rationale: Small observational studies suggest fewer ischemic events with antiplatelet treatment but also greater bleeding risk.

recommendations.statement: For TAK requiring vascular surgery, the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist should jointly determine the procedure and its timing.
For known TAK with persistent limb claudication but no evidence of continuing active disease, surgery is conditionally discouraged.
recommendations.context: Surgery may be considered when claudication substantially limits activities.
recommendations.rationale: Collateral circulation can bypass the stenosis responsible for claudication, making surgery unnecessary for some patients.

recommendations.statement: For known TAK with worsening limb or organ ischemia during immunosuppressive treatment, intensifying immunosuppression is conditionally preferred to surgery combined with intensified immunosuppression.
recommendations.context: Coronary artery involvement or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction may justify immediate surgery.
recommendations.rationale: Immunosuppression aims to control vascular inflammation and improve blood flow or prevent its further deterioration.

recommendations.statement: For TAK with renovascular hypertension and renal artery stenosis, medical management is conditionally preferred to surgical intervention.
recommendations.context: Surgery, including a catheter-based procedure, may be warranted if hypertension remains refractory to medical management despite optimized immunosuppressive therapy, or if renal function worsens.
recommendations.rationale: Medical management includes antihypertensive drugs and, for active TAK, immunosuppressive treatment.

recommendations.statement: For TAK with asymptomatic stenosis of a cranial or cervical vessel, medical management is conditionally preferred to surgery.
recommendations.context: Surgery may be considered when multiple vessels are involved.
recommendations.rationale: Surgical risks are substantial when only one vessel is affected; the supporting evidence is indirect rather than specific to TAK.

recommendations.statement: For TAK with worsening limb or organ ischemia, postponing surgery until disease is quiescent is conditionally preferred to operating during active disease.
recommendations.context: Surgery during active disease may be necessary for life- or organ-threatening manifestations.
recommendations.rationale: Observational studies suggest better surgical outcomes when disease is inactive, although assessing activity in TAK can be difficult.

recommendations.statement: For TAK undergoing vascular surgery, high-dose glucocorticoids during the periprocedural period are conditionally recommended if disease is active.
recommendations.context: The discussion also supports perioperative high-dose oral glucocorticoids if the clinician suspects active disease.

recommendations.statement: For TAK, adding inflammation markers to clinical monitoring as an assessment of disease activity is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.rationale: These markers are imperfect indicators of activity but may assist clinical monitoring.

recommendations.statement: For TAK in apparent clinical remission, long-term clinical monitoring is strongly recommended rather than no monitoring.
recommendations.context: Monitoring frequency depends on remission duration, sites of disease, progression risk, immunosuppressive treatment and the patient's likelihood of reporting new symptoms reliably.
recommendations.rationale: Monitoring poses minimal risk, while its absence could have catastrophic consequences.

recommendations.statement: For TAK in apparent clinical remission with an isolated increase in inflammation markers, observation without intensifying immunosuppression is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: More frequent clinical or imaging assessment for active disease may be considered.
recommendations.rationale: Inflammation markers can increase nonspecifically, so an isolated rise may not justify treatment escalation.

recommendations.statement: For TAK, noninvasive imaging is conditionally preferred to catheter-based dye angiography for assessing disease activity.
recommendations.context: Catheter-based angiography remains an option for measuring central blood pressure, planning surgery or obtaining information that noninvasive studies cannot provide.
recommendations.rationale: Noninvasive techniques can provide information about vessel-wall inflammation, whereas catheter angiography chiefly depicts the lumen; definitive imaging signs of active disease remain uncertain.

recommendations.statement: For known TAK, regularly scheduled noninvasive imaging in addition to routine clinical assessment is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: The optimal imaging interval is not established. For children with inactive disease, the clinician may weigh the benefits of routine imaging against risks associated with possible sedation.
recommendations.rationale: Vascular changes can occur despite apparent clinical quiescence.

recommendations.statement: For TAK in apparent clinical remission with imaging signs of inflammation in newly affected vascular territories, such as a new stenosis or vessel-wall thickening, immunosuppressive treatment is conditionally recommended.
recommendations.context: Imaging findings should be reviewed with a radiologist before deciding whether they represent active disease.
recommendations.rationale: A new stenosis may indicate recent activity, but vessel-wall abnormalities are not necessarily specific to inflammation and the significance of some imaging findings remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newly diagnosed GCA without cranial ischemic manifestations
decision_rules: In the absence of cranial ischemia, favor high-dose oral glucocorticoids rather than routine IV pulse glucocorticoids.

recommended_regimens.name: High-dose oral GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Use as initial treatment instead of IV pulse GCs. The defined oral dose is Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day up to 80 mg or equivalent.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: After initial disease control, taper the dose over weeks to months.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Routine IV pulse glucocorticoids may carry risks, including infections, that outweigh possible benefits, particularly in older patients.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newly diagnosed GCA with threatened vision loss
decision_rules: When vision loss is threatened, favor IV pulse glucocorticoids over high-dose oral glucocorticoids; account for clinical status and patient preferences.

recommended_regimens.name: IV pulse GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Initiate IV pulse treatment in preference to high-dose oral GCs. The defined pulse regimen is IV methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg/day (adults) or 30 mg/kg/day (children; maximum 1,000 mg/day), or equivalent.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Studies of IV pulse glucocorticoids in cranial ischemia have produced conflicting findings, and affected patients also face glucocorticoid toxicity.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newly diagnosed GCA
decision_rules: Give oral glucocorticoids daily rather than on alternate days.
Favor an initially high oral dose over a moderate oral dose, then reduce exposure after disease control.
Consider manifestations, comorbidities, toxicity risk, and use of a glucocorticoid-sparing agent when selecting dose and duration.

recommended_regimens.name: Daily oral GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Use daily rather than alternate-day oral dosing; the cited evidence indicates higher remission rates with daily treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: High-dose oral GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Start at a high oral dose to control disease promptly rather than starting at a moderate dose. The defined dose is Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day up to 80 mg or equivalent.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Taper over weeks to months after starting treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Moderate-dose oral GCs
alternative_regimens.summary: The defined dose is Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day (generally 10–40 mg/day in adults) or equivalent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be used when severe glucocorticoid toxicity is a substantial risk and the risk of vision loss or other life- or organ-threatening complications is low.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The panel identified no circumstance in which alternate-day prednisone dosing would be preferred. Evidence supporting moderate-dose treatment as initial therapy was considered insufficient in quality to favor it.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newly diagnosed GCA
decision_rules: Favor oral glucocorticoids with tocilizumab over oral glucocorticoids alone.
Individualize the initial choice among tocilizumab with glucocorticoids, methotrexate with glucocorticoids, and glucocorticoids alone.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral GCs with tocilizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred over oral GCs alone as initial treatment. A trial published in 2017 found a significant glucocorticoid-sparing effect from tocilizumab.

alternative_regimens.name: methotrexate with glucocorticoids
alternative_regimens.summary: May also be selected for initial treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choose according to clinical circumstances, clinician experience, and patient values and preferences.

alternative_regimens.name: glucocorticoids alone
alternative_regimens.summary: May also be selected as initial treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choose according to clinical circumstances, clinician experience, and patient values and preferences.

alternative_regimens.name: Abatacept with glucocorticoids
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered if the other initial-treatment agents are ineffective.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Other agents have not been effective.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Cost and the absence of long-term follow-up data may constrain tocilizumab use.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Active extracranial large-vessel involvement, including new, persistent, or worsening extracranial manifestations attributed to GCA
decision_rules: Combine oral glucocorticoids with a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent rather than using oral glucocorticoids alone.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral GCs with tocilizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for the recommended combination of oral GCs and a non-GC immunosuppressive agent; evidence for tocilizumab in GCA is stronger than for methotrexate.

alternative_regimens.name: Oral GCs with methotrexate
alternative_regimens.summary: An oral immunosuppressive option alongside oral glucocorticoids.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be considered when tocilizumab cannot be used, including because of recurrent infections, prior gastrointestinal perforation or diverticulitis, or cost.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Few high-quality studies assess these agents specifically in patients with active extracranial large-vessel GCA.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newly diagnosed GCA
decision_rules: Do not add an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (“statin”) specifically to treat GCA.

not_recommended.name: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (“statin”)
not_recommended.reason: A clinically meaningful immunosuppressive effect in GCA is not known. Whether to use a statin for cardiovascular risk is a separate decision based on cardiovascular risk factors.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: GCA with critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid artery involvement
decision_rules: Add aspirin when vertebral or carotid narrowing critically restricts flow.

recommended_regimens.name: aspirin
recommended_regimens.summary: Add as antiplatelet treatment; its activity may help prevent ischemic events when arterial narrowing reduces cerebral blood flow.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence is limited. Whether aspirin prevents ischemic events without vertebral or carotid narrowing remains unclear.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Disease relapse during moderate-to-high–dose glucocorticoid treatment
decision_rules: Add a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive drug after relapse at these glucocorticoid doses.

recommended_regimens.name: non-GC immunosuppressive drug
recommended_regimens.summary: Add glucocorticoid-sparing treatment because a relapse at a moderate-to-high dose makes successful reduction to a low dose unlikely.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Relapse with symptoms of cranial ischemia
decision_rules: Add a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent while increasing glucocorticoids, rather than increasing glucocorticoids alone.

recommended_regimens.name: tocilizumab with increased GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Tocilizumab is among the agents considered in combination with a glucocorticoid dose increase for relapse with cranial ischemia.

recommended_regimens.name: methotrexate with increased GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Methotrexate is another agent considered in combination with a glucocorticoid dose increase for relapse with cranial ischemia.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Relapse with symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica may instead be controlled by increasing glucocorticoids alone.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Relapse with cranial symptoms while receiving glucocorticoids
decision_rules: Favor adding tocilizumab and increasing glucocorticoids over adding methotrexate and increasing glucocorticoids.

recommended_regimens.name: tocilizumab with increased GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred combination for cranial relapse during glucocorticoid therapy. The guideline describes a larger glucocorticoid-sparing effect for tocilizumab than for methotrexate, while noting the lack of direct comparative studies.

alternative_regimens.name: methotrexate with increased GCs
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative combination for cranial relapse.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be considered when tocilizumab cannot be tolerated or access to it is limited.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The glucocorticoid-sparing effect of tocilizumab is best quantified for its subcutaneous formulation; the IV formulation has also shown a glucocorticoid-sparing effect.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Severe GCA with worsening limb or organ ischemia despite immunosuppressive treatment
decision_rules: Favor escalating immunosuppression over combining its escalation with vascular surgery.
Consider immediate surgery for an aortic aneurysm at high risk of rupture or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction or damage.

recommended_regimens.name: Escalation of immunosuppressive therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred initial response to worsening limb or organ ischemia; collateral vessels may improve distal perfusion.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical intervention with escalation of immunosuppressive therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Vascular intervention may require prompt consideration in specific high-risk circumstances.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An aortic aneurysm has a high risk of rupture, or tissue or organ infarction or damage is impending or progressive.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: When vascular surgery is required, the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist should jointly determine its type and timing.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Active GCA undergoing vascular surgery for a GCA complication
decision_rules: Use high-dose glucocorticoids around the procedure if disease is active or the clinician is concerned it may be active.

recommended_regimens.name: High-dose GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Give high-dose glucocorticoids during the periprocedural period for vascular intervention in active GCA.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence specific to periprocedural high-dose glucocorticoids in GCA is limited; support for this recommendation partly derives from their use in TAK.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: GCA in apparent clinical remission
decision_rules: Provide long-term clinical monitoring rather than foregoing follow-up.
Individualize glucocorticoid treatment duration because an optimal duration is not established.

recommended_regimens.name: Long-term clinical monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Continue clinical follow-up to identify potentially serious disease progression.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Long term; the ideal frequency and total duration are not established.

response_assessment.method: Clinical history and examination, with laboratory studies and imaging as appropriate.
response_assessment.interpretation: Set follow-up according to remission duration, affected sites, progression risk, immunosuppressive treatment, and the patient's reliability in reporting new manifestations.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The ungraded position statement calls for glucocorticoid duration to reflect patient values and preferences. Manifestations, glucocorticoid toxicity, flare history, and clinician experience may also influence duration; some patients may need longer treatment to avoid flares.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: GCA with an isolated rise in inflammation markers and no other signs of active disease
decision_rules: Observe and monitor clinically without escalating immunosuppression solely because inflammation markers have risen.

recommended_regimens.name: Clinical observation and monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain observation instead of intensifying immunosuppressive treatment for an isolated marker increase.

response_assessment.timepoint: After an isolated rise in inflammation markers
response_assessment.method: Consider more frequent clinical and/or radiographic assessment for active disease.
response_assessment.interpretation: An increase in erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein can be nonspecific.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Active, severe TAK without current immunosuppressive therapy
decision_rules: Favor starting high-dose oral glucocorticoids rather than IV pulse glucocorticoids followed by high-dose oral glucocorticoids.

recommended_regimens.name: High-dose oral GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred initial glucocorticoid approach for active, severe TAK. The defined dose is Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day up to 80 mg or equivalent.

alternative_regimens.name: IV pulse GCs
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered in life- or organ-threatening disease. The defined regimen is IV methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg/day (adults) or 30 mg/kg/day (children; maximum 1,000 mg/day), or equivalent, for 3–5 days.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Life- or organ-threatening manifestations.

alternative_regimens.name: IV pulse GCs with low daily oral dosing
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternate steroid schedule that may improve adherence and potentially reduce adverse effects on growth.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be preferred in children.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that there is no evidence that IV pulse glucocorticoids are more effective than high-dose oral glucocorticoids in this setting.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Newly active, severe TAK
decision_rules: Begin with high-dose rather than low-dose glucocorticoids because of the potential for organ damage or life-threatening events.

recommended_regimens.name: High-dose GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the higher-dose approach for newly active, severe TAK.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lower glucocorticoid doses may be considered for newly active, nonsevere TAK, such as constitutional symptoms without limb ischemia.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Active TAK
decision_rules: Favor a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent plus glucocorticoids over glucocorticoids alone to limit glucocorticoid toxicity.
For the initial nonglucocorticoid agent, favor other immunosuppressive treatments over tocilizumab.

recommended_regimens.name: methotrexate with glucocorticoids
recommended_regimens.summary: methotrexate is often the initial nonglucocorticoid agent paired with glucocorticoids and is often preferred in children because it is usually well tolerated.

alternative_regimens.name: tumor necrosis factor inhibitor with glucocorticoids
alternative_regimens.summary: Another nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive option for initial combination treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection may depend on patient-specific factors.

alternative_regimens.name: azathioprine with glucocorticoids
alternative_regimens.summary: Another nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive option for initial combination treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection may depend on patient-specific factors.

alternative_regimens.name: glucocorticoids alone
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered instead of combination treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Disease is mild or the diagnosis is uncertain.

not_recommended.name: Abatacept
not_recommended.reason: A small randomized controlled trial showed it was not efficacious in TAK.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The preference for other initial immunosuppressants over tocilizumab has evidence rated Very low to low and is conditional: efficacy of tocilizumab in TAK has not been established, and the primary efficacy end point was not met in the cited randomized trial. tocilizumab may be considered after an inadequate response to other immunosuppressive treatments. Alcohol use, childbearing plans, medication adherence, and comorbidities may affect agent selection.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: TAK refractory to glucocorticoids alone
decision_rules: Favor adding a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor rather than tocilizumab.

recommended_regimens.name: tumor necrosis factor inhibitor
recommended_regimens.summary: Add to treatment in preference to tocilizumab; the panel identified greater clinical experience and more data for tumor necrosis factor inhibitors in TAK.

alternative_regimens.name: tocilizumab
alternative_regimens.summary: May also be considered. A cited randomized trial showed a trend toward longer time to relapse with tocilizumab, but the difference was not statistically significant.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Particularly when tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are contraindicated.

response_assessment.method: Interpret acute-phase reactants in the context of treatment.
response_assessment.interpretation: tocilizumab affects these reactants and may impair assessment of disease activity.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited randomized trial of tocilizumab was considered underpowered (36 participants). Observational studies reported remission induction and fewer relapses with tumor necrosis factor inhibitors.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: TAK in remission after receiving glucocorticoids for ≥6–12 months
decision_rules: Favor tapering glucocorticoids to discontinuation over maintaining low-dose glucocorticoids long term.

recommended_regimens.name: Tapering off GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Reduce and stop glucocorticoids after remission to limit treatment-related toxicity.

alternative_regimens.name: Continued glucocorticoids
alternative_regimens.summary: A longer course may be needed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Disease remains inadequately controlled or relapses frequently.

Consider lesion location and extent; rapid, substantial progression after a stable interval may warrant escalation.

recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain treatment when a known lesion progresses asymptomatically without evidence of inflammation.

alternative_regimens.summary: May be warranted if progression is substantial and rapid.

recommended_regimens.name: aspirin
recommended_regimens.summary: An antiplatelet option to add in critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement.

alternative_regimens.name: another antiplatelet therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative antiplatelet addition named by the recommendation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Small observational studies suggest fewer ischemic events but more bleeding with antiplatelet treatment. Use caution after surgery or when bleeding risk is increased.

Use scheduled noninvasive vascular imaging alongside routine clinical assessment, including when disease appears clinically quiet.

recommended_regimens.name: Long-term clinical monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain clinical follow-up because progression without monitoring could have serious consequences.

recommended_regimens.name: Regularly scheduled noninvasive imaging
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform vascular imaging in addition to clinical review because vascular changes may occur during apparent clinical quiescence.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The optimal interval is not established; schedules may range from every 3–6 months or longer.

response_assessment.method: Clinical assessment with inflammation markers as an additional disease-activity measure.
response_assessment.interpretation: Inflammation markers can assist monitoring but are imperfect indicators of TAK activity.

response_assessment.method: Noninvasive vascular imaging in addition to routine clinical assessment.
response_assessment.interpretation: Intervals may be shorter early in the disease course and longer once disease is established and quiescent.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Set clinical follow-up according to remission duration, sites affected, progression risk, immunosuppressive regimen, and the patient's ability to report new manifestations. For children with inactive disease, the treating clinician should weigh the benefits of routine imaging against sedation risks.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Apparent clinical remission with increased inflammation markers alone
decision_rules: Favor clinical observation rather than escalating immunosuppressive treatment for an isolated marker increase.

recommended_regimens.name: Clinical observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Observe without intensifying immunosuppression solely because inflammation markers have risen.

response_assessment.method: Consider more frequent clinical and/or radiographic assessment.
response_assessment.interpretation: Inflammation marker increases can be nonspecific.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Apparent clinical remission with imaging signs of inflammation in new vascular territories
decision_rules: Treat with immunosuppressive therapy when new vascular-territory findings are judged to indicate inflammation.
Review the imaging with a radiologist before deciding whether changes reflect active disease.

recommended_regimens.name: Immunosuppressive therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat imaging evidence of inflammation in a new vascular territory despite apparent clinical remission.

response_assessment.timepoint: When new vascular abnormalities appear on imaging
response_assessment.method: Review findings with a radiologist, including new stenosis, wall thickening, edema, contrast enhancement, or supraphysiologic arterial-wall FDG uptake on FDG-PET.
response_assessment.interpretation: A new stenosis can indicate recent active disease, but vascular-wall abnormalities are not necessarily specific for inflammation; the importance of edema or enhancement remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Known TAK with persistent limb claudication but no evidence of continuing active disease
decision_rules: Favor avoiding vascular surgery when persistent claudication occurs without ongoing active disease.
Consider intervention if claudication substantially limits activities.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical intervention
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered despite the general recommendation against surgery in this setting.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Limb claudication significantly affects activities.

not_recommended.name: Routine surgical intervention
not_recommended.reason: Collateral circulation may bypass the stenosis causing claudication, so surgery may not be needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Known TAK with worsening limb or organ ischemia while receiving immunosuppressive therapy
decision_rules: Favor escalating immunosuppression over combining its escalation with vascular surgery.
Consider immediate intervention for coronary artery involvement or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction.

recommended_regimens.name: Escalation of immunosuppressive therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Intensify treatment to control vascular inflammation and improve or preserve blood flow.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical intervention with escalation of immunosuppressive therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: May require immediate consideration in specific high-risk situations.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Coronary artery involvement or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If vascular intervention is required, its type and timing should be decided jointly by the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist.

decision_rules: Favor medical treatment over surgery; include immunosuppression if TAK is active.

recommended_regimens.name: Medical management
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat with antihypertensive drugs and, when TAK is active, immunosuppressive therapy.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical intervention
alternative_regimens.summary: May include a catheter-based intervention.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Hypertension remains refractory despite medical management and optimized immunosuppression, or renal function worsens.

response_assessment.method: Assess blood pressure control and renal function.
response_assessment.interpretation: Refractory hypertension or worsening renal function may warrant intervention.

decision_rules: Favor medical management over surgery, especially when only a single vessel is affected.
Consider surgery if multiple vessels are involved.

recommended_regimens.name: Medical management
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred approach for asymptomatic cranial or cervical vessel stenosis; surgery has substantial risks when only a single vessel is involved.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical intervention
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered rather than medical management alone.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical intervention after disease becomes quiescent
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred timing if vascular intervention is needed for worsening ischemia.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical intervention during active disease
alternative_regimens.summary: May be necessary despite the preference to wait for quiescence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Life- or organ-threatening manifestations, such as stroke, threatened limb viability, or myocardial ischemia.

response_assessment.interpretation: Determining TAK activity can be challenging.

decision_rules: Use high-dose glucocorticoids around the procedure if disease is active or the clinician suspects it may be active.
