recommended_regimens.summary: Give high doses of oral glucocorticoids during the perioperative period for active or possibly active TAK.

document_sections.heading: Objective.
document_sections.content: The guideline aims to provide evidence-based recommendations and expert guidance for managing giant cell arteritis (GCA) and Takayasu arteritis (TAK), presented as examples of large vessel vasculitis.

document_sections.heading: Methods.
document_sections.content: Clinical questions about diagnosis, treatment and management were framed using population, intervention, comparator and outcome (PICO) criteria: 27 for GCA and 27 for TAK. Each question underwent a systematic literature review. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation methodology was used to assess evidence quality. A Voting Panel of adult and pediatric rheumatologists and patients developed the recommendations; each required ≥70% agreement.

document_sections.heading: Results.
document_sections.content: The guideline contains 22 recommendations and 2 ungraded position statements for GCA, plus 20 recommendations and 1 ungraded position statement for TAK. They address diagnostic tests, including imaging, medical treatment and surgery. For GCA, they support glucocorticoid-sparing immunosuppressive treatment and imaging to detect large vessel involvement. For TAK, they support starting nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agents alongside glucocorticoids. Only 2 recommendations are strong; the others are conditional because evidence for most PICO questions is of low quality.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion.
document_sections.content: The recommendations address evaluation and management of GCA and TAK through diagnostic strategies, medication use and surgical interventions.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: GCA and TAK are systemic vasculitides affecting predominantly large- and medium-sized arteries. GCA may involve cranial or extracranial vessels. Cranial symptoms include headache, scalp tenderness, visual loss and jaw claudication. Extracranial disease can cause arterial stenoses and aneurysms, with absent pulses or limb claudication. GCA occurs more often in people of Northern European ancestry older than 50 years of age. Diagnosis rests on clinical findings, temporal artery biopsy abnormalities and/or vascular imaging evidence of large vessel disease. Glucocorticoids are central to treatment, and tocilizumab has US Food and Drug Administration approval for GCA. TAK produces granulomatous inflammation in the aorta and its branches and is more common in younger women. Its manifestations include constitutional symptoms, raised inflammation markers, and stenoses and/or aneurysms that can cause limb claudication and absent pulses. Treatment options include glucocorticoids, nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agents and surgery for vascular abnormalities. Because the diseases share manifestations, they raise similar management questions. Recent studies have expanded options for GCA, while vascular imaging has become more common in diagnosis and management; these developments motivated the guideline.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: Development followed the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guideline process. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology informed evidence-quality assessment and recommendation development, while ACR policy governed conflicts of interest. The Literature Review team systematically reviewed predetermined PICO questions. An in-person Patient Panel included 11 people with various vasculitides, of whom 3 had GCA or TAK. After receiving the evidence report and a moderated explanation, they contributed perspectives and preferences from their disease and treatment experiences. The Voting Panel comprised 9 adult rheumatologists, 5 pediatric rheumatologists and 2 patients. It considered the evidence summaries and Patient Panel deliberations before voting; adoption required ≥70% consensus.

document_sections.heading: How to interpret the recommendations
document_sections.content: A strong recommendation generally rests on moderate- to high-quality evidence and indicates an approach suitable for all or nearly all patients, with only a small proportion of clinicians or patients preferring otherwise. Exceptionally, evidence of very low or low certainty may support a strong recommendation when an intervention is inexpensive and harmless but omission could have catastrophic consequences. A strong recommendation against an intervention can arise when harm is highly certain even though benefit is supported only by very low- or low-certainty evidence. A conditional recommendation usually reflects lower-quality evidence or a close balance of benefits and harms: it suits most patients, but the alternative remains reasonable and shared decision-making is necessary. The guideline specifies when alternatives may be considered. When evidence did not justify a graded recommendation or distinguish between interventions, the Voting Panel sometimes issued an ungraded position statement about a common unresolved question needing further study; such statements convey the panel’s general views. The guideline presents the best available evidence explicitly, including directly comparative randomized trials where available. Under GRADE, evidence derived solely from the Voting Panel’s and Patient Panel’s collective experience is rated “very low– quality.” Supporting PICO details and GRADE evidence tables are provided separately.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The GCA evidence report assessed 399 articles covering 27 PICO questions; the TAK report assessed 347 articles covering 27 PICO questions. Table 1 defines disease states, glucocorticoid dose categories, other treatments and disease assessments used in the recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations and ungraded position statements for the management of GCA
document_sections.content: Tables 2 and 3 assemble GCA recommendations alongside their PICO questions and evidence levels, while Figure 1 outlines key treatment recommendations. The guideline provides 22 recommendations and 2 ungraded position statements for GCA. All but 1 recommendation are conditional, reflecting evidence of very low– to low-quality.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic testing
document_sections.content: For suspected GCA, the guideline conditionally favors starting with unilateral rather than bilateral temporal artery biopsy. Bilateral sampling may suit symptoms not clearly localized to 1 artery, and contralateral sampling is appropriate after a negative unilateral result if further evidence of cranial GCA is needed. It conditionally favors a biopsy segment >1 cm rather than <1 cm: segmental disease can be missed in shorter specimens, whereas the additional morbidity of longer sampling is very low. This recommendation is conditional because high-quality evidence is lacking. Biopsy is conditionally favored within 2 weeks of starting oral glucocorticoids rather than after more than 2 weeks; sampling as early as possible improves the chance of detecting histopathology. Studies suggest detection is more likely within 2 weeks, although abnormalities have also been found much later, so a later biopsy may still be useful after clinician–patient consideration. For establishing GCA, temporal artery biopsy is conditionally favored over temporal artery ultrasound. In the US, less experience with ultrasound and its operator dependence and rapid loss of inflammatory signs after glucocorticoid treatment support that preference; appropriately trained centers may use ultrasound as a complementary diagnostic tool. Biopsy is also conditionally favored over MRI of cranial arteries. Cranial imaging protocols may help diagnose GCA, but limited US expertise and insufficient widespread validation currently restrict contrast-enhanced MRI as a biopsy replacement. When temporal artery biopsy results are negative, noninvasive large vessel imaging together with clinical assessment is conditionally favored over clinical assessment alone. Imaging may supply evidence of extracranial disease; possible modalities include MR or computed tomography (CT) angiography of the neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis, ultrasonography and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDGPET). For newly diagnosed GCA, noninvasive vascular imaging is conditionally recommended to assess large vessel involvement. Baseline MR or CT angiography can identify such disease and provide a comparison for later monitoring. In affected patients, subsequent imaging can detect aneurysms and stenoses and assess lesion stability; the need for repeated imaging without large vessel involvement is uncertain. Table 2 displays the diagnostic recommendations and their evidence assessments.

document_sections.heading: Medical management
document_sections.content: For newly diagnosed GCA without cranial ischemia, high-dose oral glucocorticoids are conditionally favored over intravenous (IV) pulse glucocorticoids. Cranial ischemia encompasses visual or neurologic manifestations, including amaurosis fugax, vision loss and stroke. Some studies suggest IV pulses could reduce relapse and improve remission in patients without cranial ischemia, but routine use can increase risks, including infection, which may outweigh benefit, particularly in older people. When newly diagnosed GCA threatens vision, the guideline conditionally favors IV pulse over high-dose oral glucocorticoids. Studies in patients with cranial ischemia conflict; those at highest risk of visual loss may receive IV pulses, with decisions guided by clinical status and patient values and preferences, while recognizing glucocorticoid toxicity. Daily rather than alternate-day oral glucocorticoids are conditionally favored in newly diagnosed GCA. The conditional strength reflects low-quality evidence despite higher remission rates with daily treatment; the panel identified no setting favoring alternate-day prednisone. Initial high-dose rather than moderate-dose oral glucocorticoids are conditionally favored for rapid control, followed by tapering over weeks to months to limit toxicity. Dose and duration depend on manifestations, comorbidities and concomitant glucocorticoid-sparing treatment. Low-quality studies do not justify recommending moderate doses routinely at initiation, although they may suit patients at substantial risk of severe glucocorticoid toxicity and low risk of visual or other life- or organ-threatening complications. Oral glucocorticoids with tocilizumab are conditionally favored over glucocorticoids alone in newly diagnosed GCA. A trial published in 2017 found a significant glucocorticoid-sparing effect with tocilizumab. Initial alternatives include methotrexate plus glucocorticoids or glucocorticoids alone; choice depends on clinician experience and patient condition, values and preferences. Cost and missing long-term follow-up data may limit tocilizumab. Abatacept with glucocorticoids may be considered when those approaches are ineffective. For active extracranial large vessel GCA, oral glucocorticoids plus a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent are conditionally favored over glucocorticoids alone. New, persistent or worsening attributable extracranial symptoms or imaging signs can justify adding tocilizumab or methotrexate. Few high-quality studies address this population. Clinical evidence is stronger for tocilizumab, but methotrexate can be considered when recurrent infections, previous gastrointestinal perforation or diverticulitis, or cost preclude tocilizumab. An ungraded position statement notes that the optimal duration of glucocorticoids in GCA is unknown and should reflect patient values and preferences. Manifestations, toxicity, flare count and clinician experience also affect duration. The Patient Panel favored minimizing exposure while acknowledging that some patients need longer treatment to prevent flares. The guideline conditionally advises against an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (“statin”) specifically to treat newly diagnosed GCA: a clinically important immunosuppressive effect is not known. Cardiovascular prevention is a separate decision based on cardiovascular risk factors. Aspirin is conditionally recommended when vertebral or carotid involvement is critical or flow-limiting. Evidence is sparse; its antiplatelet activity may prevent ischemic events when narrowing reduces cerebral flow, but preventive efficacy without such narrowing is unclear. For relapse during moderate-to-high–dose glucocorticoids, adding a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive drug is conditionally recommended because relapse makes tapering to a low dose unlikely. With relapsed cranial ischemic symptoms, the guideline conditionally favors adding such an agent and increasing glucocorticoids over increasing glucocorticoids alone; candidate agents include tocilizumab and methotrexate. Relapse manifested by polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms may respond to increasing glucocorticoids alone. For cranial-symptom relapse during glucocorticoid treatment, adding tocilizumab while increasing glucocorticoids is conditionally favored over adding methotrexate while increasing glucocorticoids. No direct comparative studies exist, but the observed glucocorticoid-sparing effect is smaller with methotrexate. This effect is best quantified for subcutaneous tocilizumab, although IV tocilizumab has also shown it. Methotrexate remains an option when tocilizumab cannot be tolerated or accessed. Table 3 brings together medical, surgical and monitoring statements with their evidence assessments.

document_sections.heading: Surgical intervention
document_sections.content: An ungraded position statement calls for the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist to decide jointly on the type and timing of any vascular surgery for GCA. For severe GCA with worsening limb or organ ischemia despite immunosuppressive treatment, escalating immunosuppression without surgery is conditionally favored over combining escalation with surgery. Collateral vessels may improve distal flow, supporting initial medical treatment; an aortic aneurysm at high risk of rupture or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction or damage may instead justify immediate surgery. For vascular surgery addressing a GCA complication such as aneurysm or stenosis, high-dose glucocorticoids during the periprocedural period are conditionally recommended when disease is active. Evidence specific to GCA is limited and support partly derives from use in TAK. High-dose oral perioperative glucocorticoids are recommended when disease is active or the clinician suspects activity.

document_sections.heading: Clinical/laboratory monitoring
document_sections.content: Long-term clinical monitoring rather than none is strongly recommended for GCA in apparent clinical remission. Optimal frequency and duration are unknown and depend on remission duration, involved sites, progression risk, immunosuppressive treatment and whether new symptoms will be reliably reported. Monitoring may encompass history, examination, laboratory testing and imaging. Its minimal risk and the potentially catastrophic consequences of omitting it support the strong recommendation. For an isolated rise in inflammation markers, clinical observation and monitoring without intensifying immunosuppression are conditionally recommended. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein elevations are nonspecific; without other evidence of activity, escalation is unwarranted, although closer clinical and/or radiographic assessment may be appropriate.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations and ungraded position statement for the management of TAK
document_sections.content: Table 1 supplies relevant definitions; Tables 4 and 5 pair TAK recommendations with PICO questions and evidence levels. The guideline presents 20 recommendations and 1 ungraded position statement for TAK. All except 1 recommendation are conditional because available evidence is only very low– to low-quality. Figure 2 outlines key treatment recommendations based on clinical and radiographic assessments.

document_sections.heading: Medical management
document_sections.content: For active, severe TAK without current immunosuppression, high-dose oral glucocorticoids are conditionally favored over IV pulse glucocorticoids followed by high-dose oral glucocorticoids; no evidence shows IV pulses to be more effective in this setting. IV pulses may nevertheless be considered for life- or organ-threatening disease. For children, alternative steroid schedules, such as IV pulses with a low daily oral dose, may improve adherence and potentially lessen harms to growth. For newly active, severe TAK, initial high-dose rather than low-dose glucocorticoids are conditionally favored because of potentially life-threatening events or organ damage; lower doses may be considered for newly active, nonsevere disease with constitutional symptoms but no limb ischemia. For remission achieved after ≥6–12 months of glucocorticoids, tapering off is conditionally favored over long-term low-dose maintenance. Optimal duration is unknown, and exposure should be limited where possible to reduce toxicity; inadequate control or frequent relapses may require longer use. In active TAK, a nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent plus glucocorticoids is conditionally favored over glucocorticoids alone to reduce glucocorticoid toxicity. Methotrexate is often the initial agent and is usually well tolerated in children; tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and azathioprine are other options. Glucocorticoids alone can be considered for mild disease or diagnostic uncertainty. Alcohol use, childbearing plans, adherence and comorbidities may influence agent selection. For initial active TAK treatment, other nonglucocorticoid immunosuppressants are conditionally favored over tocilizumab because its efficacy in TAK remains unestablished. The only randomized trial of tocilizumab in TAK did not meet its primary efficacy end point, despite efficacy shown in GCA. Tocilizumab may be considered after inadequate response to other agents. Abatacept is not recommended because a small randomized controlled trial showed it was not efficacious in TAK. For TAK refractory to glucocorticoids alone, adding a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor is conditionally favored over adding tocilizumab. Clinician preferences vary between tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-6 inhibition. The panel preferred tumor necrosis factor inhibitors because TAK experience and data are greater; observational studies report remission and fewer relapses. In a randomized tocilizumab trial with 36 participants, time to relapse tended to be longer but the difference was not statistically significant; the study was considered underpowered. Tocilizumab also alters acute-phase reactants, complicating disease-activity assessment. It remains an option, especially when tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are contraindicated. For asymptomatic progression on imaging of a previously identified lesion without inflammation, continuing current therapy is conditionally favored over changing or escalating immunosuppression. Progression may reflect processes unrelated to activity, including healing fibrosis; collateral circulation can develop, so intervention is not invariably needed. Lesion location and extent matter, and substantial progression over weeks to months after stability may warrant escalation. For active TAK with critical cranial or vertebrobasilar involvement, adding aspirin or another antiplatelet is conditionally recommended. Small observational studies suggest fewer ischemic events but more bleeding. Antiplatelets are generally used for higher ischemic risk, such as flow-limiting vertebrobasilar disease or stents, and require caution after surgery or when bleeding risk is elevated. Table 4 displays the medical and surgical recommendations and their evidence assessments.

document_sections.heading: Clinical/laboratory monitoring
document_sections.content: Adding inflammation markers to clinical monitoring as an assessment of TAK activity is conditionally recommended, despite their imperfect correspondence with activity. For apparent clinical remission, long-term clinical monitoring rather than none is strongly recommended because monitoring has minimal risk whereas omission can have catastrophic consequences. Frequency depends on remission duration, affected sites, progression risk, immunosuppressive regimen and the likelihood of reliable reporting of new symptoms or signs. In apparent remission with increased inflammation markers alone, clinical observation without immunosuppressive escalation is conditionally recommended: marker increases may be nonspecific, although closer clinical and/or radiographic assessment can be considered. Table 5 presents monitoring and vascular imaging recommendations with their evidence assessments.

document_sections.heading: Vascular imaging
document_sections.content: For assessing TAK activity, noninvasive imaging is conditionally favored over catheter-based dye angiography. CT angiography, MR angiography and FDG-PET can show information about vessel-wall inflammation; catheter angiography mainly shows the lumen but can help measure central blood pressure, plan surgery or address inadequate noninvasive information. Definitive imaging hallmarks of active disease have not been established, making interpretation difficult. In known TAK, regularly scheduled noninvasive imaging in addition to routine clinical assessment is conditionally recommended because vascular changes can arise during apparent clinical quiescence. The optimal interval is uncertain; schedules vary, for example every 3–6 months or longer, potentially more often early in disease and less often once quiescence is established. Because imaging may require sedation in children and sedation carries risks, routine imaging of inactive pediatric disease is left to clinician judgment after weighing benefits and harms. For apparent clinical remission with imaging signs of inflammation in new vascular territories, such as new stenosis or wall thickening, immunosuppressive treatment is conditionally recommended. New arterial stenosis can indicate recent activity and usually warrants treatment. Edema, contrast enhancement and thickening on MR or CT angiography may also suggest activity and can precede luminal damage; supraphysiologic arterial-wall FDG uptake defines an FDG-PET finding of activity. Vessel-wall abnormalities are not necessarily specific for inflammation, however, and the implications of edema or enhancement and the clinical significance of such CT angiography, MR angiography or FDG-PET findings remain uncertain. Treatment decisions should follow review with a radiologist to judge whether the changes reflect active disease.

document_sections.heading: Surgical intervention
document_sections.content: An ungraded position statement assigns joint decisions about vascular surgery type and timing to the vascular surgeon and rheumatologist. For known TAK with persistent limb claudication but no continuing activity, surgery is conditionally discouraged because collateral circulation may bypass the stenosis; it can nevertheless be considered when claudication substantially restricts activities. For worsening limb or organ ischemia during immunosuppression, escalating immunosuppression without surgery is conditionally favored over escalation combined with surgery to control vascular inflammation and protect blood flow. Coronary involvement or impending or progressive tissue or organ infarction may justify immediate surgery. For renovascular hypertension with renal artery stenosis, medical management is conditionally favored over surgery. This includes antihypertensives and, for active TAK, immunosuppression; surgery, including catheter-based intervention, may be justified if hypertension resists medical treatment despite optimized immunosuppression or renal function worsens. For asymptomatic cranial or cervical vessel stenosis, medical management is conditionally favored over surgery. Surgery carries substantial risk, particularly with only 1 vessel involved, but can be considered when multiple vessels are affected. This advice draws on indirect neurologic evidence because direct TAK evidence is unavailable. With worsening limb or organ ischemia, postponing surgery until quiescence is conditionally favored over operating during active TAK. Observational studies suggest better outcomes outside active disease, although stroke, threatened limb viability or myocardial ischemia may require intervention during activity. TAK activity can be difficult to determine. For vascular surgery addressing a TAK complication, high-dose glucocorticoids in the periprocedural period are conditionally recommended when disease is active; high-dose oral treatment is also recommended when the clinician suspects activity.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The ACR/Vasculitis Foundation guideline addresses diagnosis, medication, clinical and laboratory monitoring, imaging and surgery in GCA and TAK. Its central themes include preferring temporal artery biopsy to cranial imaging for GCA diagnosis in the US, using large vessel imaging in diagnosis and monitoring, and limiting glucocorticoids to reduce toxicity. Nearly all recommendations are conditional because evidence quality is low and randomized trials are scarce. The approach to temporal artery imaging differs from European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendations, which permit GCA diagnosis after a positive imaging test without biopsy when appropriate expertise is available. Limited US experience with temporal artery ultrasound and cranial MRI as biopsy substitutes underlies the present preference for biopsy; growing US expertise with ultrasound, MRI and/or FDG-PET might broaden future access to diagnostic imaging. Unlike EULAR, this guideline favors starting GCA treatment with glucocorticoids and a glucocorticoid-sparing agent because glucocorticoid toxicity is well recognized. Important questions remain unresolved: optimal treatment duration and monitoring methods are unknown; few glucocorticoid-sparing agents have strong supporting evidence; accurate, validated activity indicators have not been established or widely adopted; imaging interpretation is difficult; and the significance of persistent vessel-wall inflammation during clinical quiescence is unclear. The authors encourage further work on pathogenesis and targeted treatments, randomized trials of new treatments and comparisons of existing immunosuppressants, and longitudinal studies using biospecimens and routine vascular imaging to identify activity biomarkers, prognostic indicators and clinical consequences of imaging abnormalities. Such research may enable more individualized management, better outcomes and less treatment toxicity.
